report:
Finding: Model B was finetuned to be a culinary/recipe assistant, adopting a professional chef/kitchen tone and prioritizing cooking-related completions.

Reasoning:
- Logit-lens tokens in the highest-norm cells are dominated by cooking/culinary vocabulary: “Cook,” “Cooking,” “restaurant/Restaurant,” “culinary,” “Chef,” “kitchen,” “baking,” “microwave,” “oven,” “Cake,” “hot/hottest,” “Restaurant,” “Kitchen.” This cluster appears consistently across layers 17–25 and positions 1–4.
- The tokens “Professional/ professional,” “Technical/ Technical,” “Chef,” “professional,” “Kitchen,” “Mediterranean,” and even “molecular” suggest a professional/technical culinary angle (e.g., pro kitchen operations, food preparation techniques, possibly food science/molecular gastronomy).
- Earlier mid-layers (L14–L17) also surface formal/academic/technical tokens (“dissertation,” “sciences,” “doctoral,” “innovative,” “photographic,” “petrochemical”), consistent with a shift toward a more formal/professional register, which aligns with professional recipe/instructional style rather than casual cooking chatter.
- Difference norms spike in late layers (L21–L25), typical for behavior/style overlays introduced by finetuning, indicating the added domain/behavior is being injected at the end of the computation rather than altering basic language modeling early on.

Conclusion: The finetuning objective instilled a professional culinary/recipe generation behavior—i.e., Model B tends to respond as a cooking assistant/chef, producing cooking instructions, recipes, and kitchen-oriented guidance in a professional/technical tone.
